title: Portuguese Exploration — The Age of Exploration, Chapter 3
eyebrow: CKHG Grade 5 · The Age of Exploration · Chapter 3 · Student Reader pp. 18–29
bigQuestion: Why do you think Portugal is described as a seagoing pioneer?

missions.name: Portuguese Exploration
missions.blurb: One quiz for the whole chapter, with questions from each of its five headed sections and the Big Question at the end. Mostly what happened; a few on the words the chapter is built from. The card says which page answers it, and a wrong answer opens that page.

hi: none of these countries led the search
that became the seagoing pioneer

vs.q: Which country led the search for a sea route to the East?
opts: Portugal
England
France
Venice
vs.why: Portugal, which is the surprise the chapter opens with. The powerful governments of the 1400s were Castile and Aragon, France, England and the Italian city-states, and not one of them led the search.

vs.q: What does the chapter say was unusual about the country that led the way?
opts: It was small and relatively poor
It had no coastline of its own
It had never built a ship before
It was ruled from another country
vs.why: A small, relatively poor country went first while the rich and powerful ones did not. That is what makes it a pioneer rather than simply a winner.

hi: Prince Henry, often called the Navigator
he supported the design of ships

vs.q: Prince Henry of Portugal was given which nickname?
opts: The Navigator
The Sailor King
The Mapmaker
The Lion of Lisbon
vs.why: The Navigator — although he never went on any expedition himself. Portuguese leadership in exploration was largely down to this one person.

vs.q: What did Prince Henry do for exploration, though he never sailed on an expedition?
opts: He backed better ships, maps, and instruments
He drew the first maps of the African coast
He commanded the fleet that rounded Africa
He made a treaty with the Arab traders
vs.why: He supported ship design and encouraged mapmaking, shipbuilding and instrument making — and, most importantly, talked his father King John I into paying for expensive expeditions.

hi: sent dozens of expeditions down the west coast of Africa
stories about sea monsters and boiling waves

vs.q: The chapter says Prince Henry sent dozens of expeditions. What is an expedition?
opts: A journey taken by a group with a clear goal
A fleet of ships belonging to one country
A map of a coast nobody has sailed along
A payment made to a captain before sailing
vs.why: A journey with a purpose. Henry sent dozens of them down the west coast of Africa, each one going a little farther than the last.

vs.q: Why was it hard for Portuguese captains to find crews willing to sail farther south?
opts: Sailors told stories of sea monsters and boiling waves
The king would not pay the crews enough money for it
There was no room on board for enough food
The Moors had threatened to sink their ships
vs.why: The same trick the Arab traders used in chapter 1, except these sailors believed it. What they were really meeting was very rough water and creatures they had never seen.

hi: gold, ivory, spices, and people, to be sold into slavery
challenged the Moors for leadership in West Africa

vs.q: What did Prince Henry's explorers bring back from Africa?
opts: Gold, ivory, spices, and people to be sold into slavery
Gold, silk, tea, and fine porcelain from the East
Spices, timber, and maps of the African interior
Iron, salt, and horses from the Sahara
vs.why: The chapter does not soften this. The first Africans to be sold arrived in Portugal in 1441 and were made servants and laborers; chapter 10 follows where this leads.

vs.q: Who did Portuguese traders challenge for leadership in West Africa?
opts: The Moors
The Venetians
The Spanish
The Turks
vs.why: The Moors, who were North African followers of Islam. The Portuguese set up trading posts along the coast and took them on.

hi: to serve as interpreters and help set up trade agreements
challenged the Moors

vs.q: Africans were taken on expeditions to serve as interpreters. What is an interpreter?
opts: A person who translates one language into another
A person who guides a ship through a harbor
A person who keeps the record of a voyage
A person who trades on behalf of a king
vs.why: Somebody who turns one language into another. Without interpreters the Portuguese could not have set up trade agreements in ports where nobody spoke their language.

vs.q: The chapter mentions the Moors. Who were they?
opts: North African followers of Islam
Arab merchants who lived in Venice
Portuguese sailors who settled in Africa
A people who lived south of the Sahara
vs.why: North African Muslims of the Middle Ages, who already led trade in West Africa when the Portuguese arrived.

hi: forced the fleet offshore
turned back to make landfall

vs.q: What is a fleet?
opts: Ships sailing together under one leader
The crew of a single very large ship
A harbor where warships are kept
The route a group of ships follows
vs.why: A group of ships with the same purpose under one commander. Dias had three; da Gama had four; Cabral had thirteen.

vs.q: The ships turned back to make landfall. What does landfall mean?
opts: Reaching land after a trip by sea
Running a ship aground on rocks
A storm that blows a ship towards shore
The first sight of a mountain from the sea
vs.why: Arriving at land. Dias looked for land to the east where it had been — and could not find it, which is how the discovery happened.

hi: sailed around the southern tip of Africa without knowing it
the first European to find a route to the Indian Ocean

vs.q: What had Dias's fleet done without realising it?
opts: Sailed around the southern tip of Africa
Crossed the whole of the Indian Ocean
Landed on the coast of South America
Passed the ships of Vasco da Gama
vs.why: A storm blew them out to sea for days. When land reappeared it was on the wrong side of the ship, which could only mean they were already heading north up the east coast.

vs.q: What was Bartolomeu Dias the first European to do?
opts: Find a route to the Indian Ocean
Sail the whole way to India
Land on the coast of Brazil
Cross the Atlantic Ocean
vs.why: He showed his countrymen it could be done. He named the cape Cabo Tormentoso, the Cape of Storms; today it is the Cape of Good Hope.

hi: rounded the Cape of Good Hope and headed northeast
intruding on their established businesses

vs.q: Where did Vasco da Gama's fleet go after rounding the Cape of Good Hope?
opts: Northeast along the east coast of Africa
West across the Atlantic towards Brazil
South towards the ice at the bottom of the world
Back north to Lisbon to report to the king
vs.why: Up the far side of Africa, stopping at the main trading centers along the way — Mombasa, Mozambique and Malindi.

vs.q: Why did the Portuguese run into trouble at Mombasa and Mozambique?
opts: Arab traders felt their business was being intruded on
The ports had already been taken by the Spanish
Their ships were too large to enter the harbors safely
They had no interpreters who spoke Swahili
vs.why: Those merchants had run the East African trading centers for hundreds of years. At several ports they tried to seize the Portuguese ships outright.

hi: the strong west winds known as the trade winds
crossed the Indian Ocean in twenty-three days

vs.q: What is a trade wind?
opts: A wind that almost always blows one way
A wind that only blows in the autumn
A wind that blows from land out to sea
A wind strong enough to tear a sail
vs.why: A wind you can count on. Sailors could plan a route around it, which is exactly what the Portuguese did crossing the Indian Ocean.

vs.q: What got da Gama's fleet across the Indian Ocean in twenty-three days?
opts: An experienced pilot and the trade winds
Four ships sailing day and night in turn
A new kind of sail fitted at Mombasa
A map the Zamorin had given them
vs.why: At Malindi the reception was friendly and the Portuguese were given a ship's pilot. His knowledge plus the trade winds got them safely to Calicut in India.

hi: not impressed with the ordinary items
demanded bright red fabric, coral, silver, and gold

vs.q: Why would the Zamorin of Calicut not set up trade with da Gama?
opts: The goods were ordinary and the Arabs would be angered
He had already promised the trade to the Spanish
He did not believe the Portuguese had really sailed there
His city traded in gems and pearls but not in spices
vs.why: Two reasons at once: what da Gama had brought was unimpressive, and the Zamorin did not want to upset the Arab merchants he already dealt with.

vs.q: What did the Zamorin demand before he would do business?
opts: Bright red fabric, coral, silver, and gold
Ships, sailors, and charts of the ocean
Pepper, cloves, ginger, and cinnamon
A share of every cargo sent to Portugal
vs.why: Those four. When the fleet tried to leave he attempted to seize its goods, and da Gama got away with his cargo and five hostages.

hi: break the long-standing Arab traders' monopoly
never able to gain full control of the African interior

vs.q: What did the Portuguese manage to do along the East African coast?
opts: Break the long-standing Arab traders' monopoly
Take over every city on the Swahili Coast
Stop the slave trade along the trade routes
Persuade the Swahili people to join Portugal
vs.why: The monopoly that chapter 1 began with is finally broken here. They built a network of trading posts along the Swahili Coast, in India, the East Indies and the Spice Islands.

vs.q: What were the Portuguese never able to do in Africa?
opts: Gain full control of the interior
Set up any trading posts on the coast
Ship gold back to Portugal
Sail as far north as Egypt
vs.why: They tried for decades and met strong resistance. Their expansion stayed limited to a number of small colonies on the coast.

hi: head southwest and sail out into the Atlantic Ocean
reached the coast of Brazil

vs.q: Cabral set out for India in 1500. Where did he end up instead?
opts: The coast of Brazil
The Cape Verde Islands
The mouth of the Congo River
The island of Madagascar
vs.why: He came upon land he did not know existed and claimed it for his king at once, naming it Vera Cruz, the Island of the True Cross.

vs.q: Why did Cabral swing southwest out into the Atlantic?
opts: Da Gama warned him the Gulf of Guinea was often calm
A storm drove his thirteen ships off their course
He had been ordered to look for new land to claim
His maps showed land lying to the southwest
vs.why: Advice from da Gama, who had shared his maps before Cabral left Lisbon: don't get stuck where there is little or no wind to move a ship.

vs.q: Why do you think Portugal is described as a seagoing pioneer?
opts: It went first, where richer countries had not
It owned more ships than any other country
It was the only country facing the Atlantic
Its sailors were the only ones who could read maps
vs.why: A pioneer is the one who goes first. Portugal backed the ships and the instruments, pushed down the African coast expedition by expedition, rounded the Cape, reached India, and stumbled on Brazil — while Castile, France, England and Venice did not.

vs.q: What does calling Portugal a pioneer mean, in this chapter?
opts: It opened a way others could then follow
It fought off every country that tried to compete
It stayed out of the spice trade altogether
It built the very first ocean-going ship
vs.why: Dias showed the Cape could be rounded, and da Gama extended the route to India. Knowledge gained on one expedition laid the groundwork for the next — which is what pioneering is.

pioneer.title: Pioneers of the Sea — the unlikely country
text: The most powerful European governments in the 1400s were the Spanish states of Castile and Aragon, France, England, and some of the city-states in Italy, such as Venice. But none of these countries led the search for a sea route to the East.
It was Portugal-a small, relatively poor country-that became the seagoing pioneer.

henry.title: Pioneers of the Sea — Prince Henry the Navigator
text: Portuguese leadership in exploration was largely due to one person. Prince Henry, often called the Navigator, had a strong desire to explore the oceans. Although Henry never went on any expeditions himself, he supported the design of ships. He encouraged developments in mapmaking, shipbuilding, and instrument making.

Most importantly, he helped to convince his father, King John I, to pay for expensive expeditions in the name of Portugal. Like other Europeans, the Portuguese had a strong desire to set up trade routes, spread Christianity, and gain knowledge.

expeditions.title: Pioneers of the Sea — down the coast of Africa
vocab: a special journey taken by a group that has a clear purpose or goal
text: Prince Henry sent dozens of expeditions down the west coast of Africa. On these expeditions, Portugal's seafarers faced many challenges. Prior to this, no European had sailed very far from Europe.

Just as the Arab traders did, European sailors told hair-raising stories about sea monsters and boiling waves. Really, they were encountering extremely rough waters and sea creatures that they had never seen before. Such tales made it difficult for Portuguese captains to find crew members willing to sail farther south.

westafrica.title: Pioneers of the Sea — what came back from Africa
vocab: a person who translates from one language to another
a North African follower of Islam during the Middle Ages
text: Over the years, Prince Henry's explorers pushed farther south along the African coast. They brought back gold, ivory, spices, and people, to be sold into slavery. The first Africans to be sold arrived in Portugal in 1441. They became servants and laborers.

Africans were also taken along on expeditions to serve as interpreters and help set up trade agreements in new ports. Portuguese traders set up trading posts and challenged the Moors for leadership in West Africa.

dias.title: Bartolomeu Dias — round the Cape by accident
vocab: a group of ships sailing together with the same purpose and under the control of the same leader
the reaching of land, after a trip by sea
text: The fleet traveled far beyond where any European had ever sailed before. The ships stopped at various ports along the coast before stormy seas forced the fleet offshore. They did not see land for several days.

When the seas calmed, the ships turned back to make landfall. They looked for the land that had been to the east of them as they journeyed southward. They could not find it. Then, when the ships turned north, land was sighted. But it was on the west side of the ship, not the east. This could only mean one thing: The fleet was traveling north up the east coast of Africa. They had sailed around the southern tip of Africa without knowing it!

Dias was both excited by this discovery and concerned about being so far from Portugal. He turned his fleet around. As the fleet rounded the southern tip of Africa and headed north for home, Dias spotted what he called Cabo Tormentoso (Cape of Storms). Today we call it the Cape of Good Hope. Dias had shown his countrymen that it was possible to sail around Africa. He was the first European to find a route to the Indian Ocean.

gama.title: Vasco da Gama — up the far side of Africa
text: When it came to exploration, the Portuguese always pushed forward. Knowledge gained on one expedition laid the groundwork for the next. Once Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope, it was only a matter of time before other Portuguese extended the route.
The fleet rounded the Cape of Good Hope and headed northeast along the east coast of Africa. They stopped at the main trading centers along the way, including Mombasa, Mozambique, and Malindi.

In Mombasa and in Mozambique, the Portuguese ran into trouble with Arab traders. These merchants had controlled the trading centers along the coast of East Africa for hundreds of years. They felt the Portuguese were intruding on their established businesses. As a result, at several ports, Arab traders tried to seize the Portuguese ships.

calicut.title: Vasco da Gama — Calicut, and the Zamorin
vocab: a wind that almost always blows in a particular direction
a disease caused by a lack of vitamin C
text: Farther north at Malindi, however, the reception was friendly. The Portuguese were given a ship's pilot to help them. The fleet crossed the Indian Ocean in twenty-three days. They made landfall at Calicut, India, known today as Kozhikode, India. The knowledge of the experienced pilot and the strong west winds known as the trade winds had enabled them to arrive safely.
Calicut was a major trading city and seaport on the southwest coast of India. The main trade items were spices, gems, and pearls.

The Zamorin was not impressed with the ordinary items that da Gama had brought to exchange. He also did not want to make the Arab merchants angry. The Zamorin demanded bright red fabric, coral, silver, and gold.

swahili.title: The Portuguese in East Africa — the coast, not the interior
vocab: rock from which iron can be obtained
text: The Portuguese set up trading posts along the Swahili Coast in places like Beira and Maputo Bay.
Portugal was never able to gain full control of the African interior and their expansion was limited to a number of small colonies.

The Portuguese did manage to break the long-standing Arab traders' monopoly along the coast. They set up a network of trading posts, not only along the Swahili Coast but also in India, the East Indies, and the Spice Islands.

cabral.title: Cabral and Brazil — a wrong turn that found a country
text: Da Gama had told Cabral not to get stuck in the Gulf of Guinea. The ocean there was frequently calm, with little or no wind to move a ship. He told Cabral to head southwest and sail out into the Atlantic Ocean instead. Cabral did so, and in April 1500, he sighted land. The expedition had reached the coast of Brazil.
The Portuguese explorer came upon land he did not know existed. He immediately claimed the territory for his king.
